assessment.rationale: This variant is a clean, minimal wire shell with deterministic bytes and explicit pCID dispatch, but for replay-outside-conditions it mostly pushes the real control points into unspecified wrapper or payload protocols. That makes the authority boundary clear, yet leaves recipient, epoch, geography, session binding, and peer-local anti-replay records undefined. The unknown-best-effort policy is a notable risk when an unrecognized wrapper may carry the very access conditions that should block reuse.
strengths: Deterministic CBOR bytes make exact-envelope hashing, signing, and duplicate comparison straightforward.
The spec clearly separates base-envelope duties from wrapper or payload protocols, so replay logic is not hidden in the transport shell.
It avoids a central pCID authority and supports protocol evolution through pCID-selected wrappers.
weaknesses: The base format has no built-in audience, geography, expiry, nonce, or session binding for conditional release.
No concrete feed or local-state mechanism is defined for detecting stale or unauthorized reuse.
Unknown-best-effort salvage can expose payload bytes even when the guarding wrapper semantics are not understood.
risks: Mallory can replay previously valid bytes verbatim unless higher-layer protocols add freshness and seen-state checks.
Implementations may operationalize salvaged payload from unknown wrappers and bypass access conditions.
Different handlers may enforce conditional-release semantics inconsistently, weakening interoperability and later audit.
open_questions: What concrete wrapper or payload protocol binds a content reference to audience, geography, expiry, or session context?
Should unknown-best-effort be narrowed or disabled when the outer pCID may carry access-control conditions?
What peer-local record or feed lets Dave and Carol later prove a replay was stale or outside conditions without relying on a central authority?
assessment.authority_boundary: Evidence only; does not settle PromiseGrid design.
